title: PostgreSQL LATERAL Join: Examples, Top-N per Group and Errors
description: Learn PostgreSQL LATERAL join with real examples: top-N per group, LEFT JOIN LATERAL ON true, functions, common errors and the index that makes it fast.

reviewNotes: Regular Saturday article (not a series part). Docs followed: PostgreSQL 18.6 documentation. TESTED ON PostgreSQL 16.15 (Ubuntu 16.15-0ubuntu0.24.04.1) on Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, NOT 18: the PGDG repo was reachable, but postgresql-18 needs liburing2, which comes from the Ubuntu archive, and the sandbox could not reach that archive. All query results and error messages are real output from 16.15; LATERAL behaviour is unchanged between 16 and 18 per the docs and the 18 release notes. data.text: A LATERAL join in PostgreSQL lets a subquery in the FROM clause use columns from tables listed before it. PostgreSQL runs that subquery once for each row on the left side, so you can write things like "the latest 2 orders for each customer" in one clear query. Without the LATERAL keyword, the same subquery fails with an error.

This tutorial shows how LATERAL works, the two join forms you will use most (CROSS JOIN LATERAL and LEFT JOIN LATERAL), top-N per group, set-returning functions, the real error messages you will hit, and the one index that makes these queries fast. Every query below was run and the output is copied as it came out.
What is a LATERAL join in PostgreSQL?

Normally each subquery in FROM is evaluated on its own. It cannot see any other table in the same FROM list. Putting LATERAL in front of the subquery removes that wall: the subquery may refer to columns of FROM items that appear before it.

Think of it as a loop. For each row of the left table, PostgreSQL plugs that row's values into the subquery, runs it, and joins whatever rows come back to that left row. Then it moves to the next left row. A correlated subquery in the SELECT list works the same way, but it may return only one column and one row. A LATERAL subquery may return many columns and many rows.

content: Can use ORDER BY ... LIMIT n
Keeps left rows with no match
Only with LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true

data.text: For a function call in FROM, such as generate_series() or unnest(), the keyword is optional. The function's arguments can refer to earlier FROM items anyway, so LATERAL is only a noise word there. You need it for subqueries.
Sample setup

Create a scratch database with sudo -u postgres createdb shop, connect with sudo -u postgres psql -d shop, and run the script below. Customer 4 (Karan) has no orders on purpose, so you can see how each join form treats a customer with nothing to join.

data.code:
CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id int PRIMARY KEY,
  name        text NOT NULL,
  city        text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id    int PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES customers,
  order_date  date NOT NULL,
  amount      numeric(10,2) NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO customers VALUES
  (1, 'Asha',   'Pune'),
  (2, 'Ravi',   'Chennai'),
  (3, 'Meena',  'Delhi'),
  (4, 'Karan',  'Mumbai');

INSERT INTO orders VALUES
  (101, 1, '2026-09-02', 1200.00),
  (102, 1, '2026-09-18',  450.00),
  (103, 1, '2026-10-05', 3100.00),
  (104, 2, '2026-08-21',  990.00),
  (105, 2, '2026-10-11', 2200.00),
  (106, 3, '2026-10-01',  780.00),
  (107, 3, '2026-10-20', 1500.00),
  (108, 3, '2026-10-25',  300.00);
data.caption: Sample customers and orders tables

data.text: Why the subquery fails without LATERAL
Start with the mistake almost everyone makes first. You want each customer's two biggest orders, so you write a subquery in FROM that filters on the outer customer:

data.code:
SELECT c.name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM customers c,
     (SELECT order_id, amount
        FROM orders
       WHERE orders.customer_id = c.customer_id
       ORDER BY amount DESC
       LIMIT 2) o;
data.caption: A subquery in FROM that refers to c, without LATERAL

data.code:
ERROR:  invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "c"
LINE 5:        WHERE orders.customer_id = c.customer_id
                                          ^
DETAIL:  There is an entry for table "c", but it cannot be referenced from this part of the query.
HINT:  To reference that table, you must mark this subquery with LATERAL.
data.caption: Output

data.text: The HINT tells you the fix. The subquery was evaluated on its own, so c did not exist inside it. Adding LATERAL is all it takes.
CROSS JOIN LATERAL: top-N rows per group
This is the most common use of LATERAL: the top N child rows for every parent row. The ORDER BY and LIMIT sit inside the subquery, so the limit applies per customer, not to the whole result.

data.code:
SELECT c.name, o.order_id, o.order_date, o.amount
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT order_id, order_date, amount
    FROM orders
   WHERE orders.customer_id = c.customer_id
   ORDER BY amount DESC
   LIMIT 2
) o
ORDER BY c.name, o.amount DESC;
data.caption: Two biggest orders for each customer
Output

data.text: Each customer gets at most two rows, ordered by amount. Notice that Karan is missing. CROSS JOIN LATERAL behaves like an inner join: when the subquery returns no rows for a customer, that customer drops out of the result.
You can also write FROM customers c, LATERAL (...) o with a comma. It means the same thing as CROSS JOIN LATERAL; pick one style and use it consistently.
LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true: keep every left row
To keep customers who have no orders, use LEFT JOIN LATERAL. A left join needs a join condition, but the real filtering already happens inside the subquery, so the condition is simply ON true.

data.code:
SELECT c.name, last_order.order_id, last_order.order_date, last_order.amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT order_id, order_date, amount
    FROM orders
   WHERE orders.customer_id = c.customer_id
   ORDER BY order_date DESC
   LIMIT 1
) last_order ON true
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
data.caption: Latest order per customer, including customers with no orders
Output

data.text: Karan now appears with NULLs in the order columns. This "latest row per group" query is also something DISTINCT ON can do; see PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON for that approach. LATERAL wins when you need more than one row per group or want to keep groups with no rows.
Use CROSS JOIN LATERAL when a left row without matches should disappear, and LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true when it must stay. Most report queries want the LEFT form.
Return several computed columns per row
A scalar subquery in the SELECT list can return only one column. If you try two, PostgreSQL stops you:

data.code:
SELECT c.name,
       (SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders
         WHERE orders.customer_id = c.customer_id
         ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT 1)
FROM customers c;
data.caption: Two columns from a scalar subquery

data.code:
ERROR:  subquery must return only one column
LINE 2:        (SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders
               ^
data.caption: Output

data.text: A LATERAL subquery returns as many columns as you like, and you compute them in one pass over each customer's orders instead of three separate subqueries:

data.code:
SELECT c.name, s.order_count, s.total_amount, s.first_order
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT count(*)        AS order_count,
         sum(amount)     AS total_amount,
         min(order_date) AS first_order
    FROM orders
   WHERE orders.customer_id = c.customer_id
) s ON true
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
data.caption: Order count, total and first order date per customer
Output

data.text: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns exactly one row, so Karan gets count = 0 and NULL for the sum and date. Wrap them in coalesce() if your report needs 0 instead of NULL.
Reuse a calculated value in the same query

You cannot refer to a column alias from the SELECT list elsewhere in that same SELECT list. A chain of small LATERAL subqueries gets around this: each one can use the columns computed by the one before it. Here we work out 18% GST once and reuse it:

data.caption: Compute once, reuse in the next step
Output

data.text: Each subquery without a FROM returns exactly one row, so these joins never add or remove rows. They just give names to intermediate values, which keeps long formulas readable.
LATERAL with set-returning functions

A set-returning function returns several rows, like generate_series(), unnest() or jsonb_array_elements(). Joining one to a table and passing a column as its argument is a lateral join. This example splits order 103 into three monthly EMI (instalment) rows:

data.code:
SELECT o.order_id, o.amount, emi.n AS installment,
       (o.order_date + emi.n * interval '1 month')::date AS due_date,
       round(o.amount / 3, 2) AS emi_amount
FROM orders o
CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(1, 3) AS emi(n)
WHERE o.order_id = 103;
data.caption: Three monthly instalments for one order
Output

data.text: For functions the LATERAL keyword is optional: CROSS JOIN generate_series(1, 3) AS emi(n) returns the same three rows. Many developers still write it so readers can see that the function runs per row. When the function's arguments use columns from the left table (for example unnest(o.tags)), it is evaluated for each left row either way.
Common mistakes
1. Forgetting the LATERAL keyword on a subquery
You get invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table with the HINT "you must mark this subquery with LATERAL". Add LATERAL before the opening bracket.
2. Leaving out ON true with LEFT JOIN LATERAL

data.caption: LEFT JOIN without a join condition
Output

data.text: LEFT JOIN always needs ON or USING. Add ON true after the alias. CROSS JOIN LATERAL does not take a condition.
3. Using RIGHT or FULL JOIN with a lateral reference

data.caption: RIGHT JOIN to a LATERAL subquery that refers to c

data.code:
ERROR:  invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "c"
LINE 4: ...T order_id FROM orders WHERE orders.customer_id = c.customer...
                                                             ^
DETAIL:  The combining JOIN type must be INNER or LEFT for a LATERAL reference.
data.caption: Output

data.text: The documentation explains why: the table supplying the columns must be INNER or LEFT joined to the LATERAL item, or there is no defined set of rows to run the subquery for. The syntax parses, but the reference is not allowed. Rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped, or as a normal join.
4. Putting LIMIT outside the subquery
LIMIT 2 after the final ORDER BY limits the whole result to two rows. For "two per customer", the LIMIT must be inside the LATERAL subquery.
5. Referring to a table that comes later in FROM
A LATERAL item can only see FROM items to its left (and, inside a JOIN, the left side of that JOIN). Put the table that supplies the values first.
Performance: the index that makes LATERAL fast

Because the subquery runs once per left row, its cost is multiplied by the number of left rows. The plan is usually a Nested Loop with the subquery on the inner side. If the inner side has to scan the whole child table, that gets slow quickly.
To show the effect, we built a larger copy of the data: 500 customers and 100,000 orders in tables customers_big and orders_big, then asked for each customer's latest order:

data.caption: Test data: 500 customers, 200 orders each

data.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS OFF, COSTS OFF)
SELECT c.name, lo.order_id, lo.order_date
FROM customers_big c
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders_big
   WHERE orders_big.customer_id = c.customer_id
   ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT 1
) lo ON true;
data.caption: Latest order per customer, no index on orders_big

data.code:
Nested Loop Left Join (actual time=138.301..2633.021 rows=500 loops=1)
   ->  Seq Scan on customers_big c (actual time=0.019..0.540 rows=500 loops=1)
   ->  Limit (actual time=4.992..4.992 rows=1 loops=500)
         ->  Sort (actual time=4.986..4.986 rows=1 loops=500)
               Sort Key: orders_big.order_date DESC
               Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 25kB
               ->  Seq Scan on orders_big (actual time=0.016..4.933 rows=200 loops=500)
                     Filter: (customer_id = c.customer_id)
                     Rows Removed by Filter: 99800
 Planning Time: 0.327 ms
 Execution Time: 2650.975 ms
data.caption: Output (plan without the index)

data.text: Read loops=500: the inner Seq Scan ran 500 times, each time reading all 100,000 orders and throwing away 99,800 of them. Now add an index that matches both the filter and the sort:

data.code:
CREATE INDEX orders_big_cust_date_idx
    ON orders_big (customer_id, order_date DESC);
data.caption: Composite index matching WHERE and ORDER BY

data.code:
Nested Loop Left Join (actual time=0.045..1.869 rows=500 loops=1)
   ->  Seq Scan on customers_big c (actual time=0.011..0.060 rows=500 loops=1)
   ->  Limit (actual time=0.003..0.003 rows=1 loops=500)
         ->  Index Scan using orders_big_cust_date_idx on orders_big (actual time=0.003..0.003 rows=1 loops=500)
               Index Cond: (customer_id = c.customer_id)
 Planning Time: 0.368 ms
 Execution Time: 1.923 ms
data.caption: Output (same query after creating the index)

data.text: The Sort node is gone. Each of the 500 loops walks straight to the newest entry for that customer and stops after one row because of the LIMIT. On our test machine the time dropped from about 2.6 seconds to about 2 milliseconds; your numbers will differ, but the shape of the plan is what matters.

From PostgreSQL 18, EXPLAIN ANALYZE includes buffer usage automatically, which is why the examples pass BUFFERS OFF to keep the plan short. PostgreSQL 18 also reports the number of index lookups on index scan nodes, so you will see a few extra lines compared with older versions.
Drop the test tables when you are done with DROP TABLE orders_big, customers_big;. Other practical points:

items.content: Rule of thumb for top-N per group: index the child table on (join column, sort column in the same direction), for example (customer_id, order_date DESC).
LATERAL shines when the left side is small or filtered and each group has many child rows: it reads only N rows per group.

When you need the top N for almost every group of a big table, a single pass with row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) can be cheaper than thousands of index lookups. Compare both with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on your own data.
Filter the left table as early as possible (in its WHERE clause), because every left row costs one execution of the subquery.

data.text: Here is the window-function version of the earlier "two biggest orders" query, for comparison. It returns the same six rows. Learn more about window functions in Mastering SQL Window Functions.

data.code:
SELECT name, order_id, order_date, amount
FROM (
  SELECT c.name, o.order_id, o.order_date, o.amount,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id
                            ORDER BY o.amount DESC) AS rn
    FROM customers c
    JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
) ranked
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY name, amount DESC;
data.caption: Top 2 orders per customer with row_number()
Output

data.text: Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between LATERAL join and a subquery in PostgreSQL?

A plain subquery in FROM runs once, on its own, and cannot see other tables in the FROM list. A LATERAL subquery runs once per left row and can use that row's columns. Compared with a correlated subquery in SELECT, LATERAL can return many rows and many columns.
Is LATERAL the same as CROSS APPLY in SQL Server or Oracle?

Yes, in effect. CROSS JOIN LATERAL matches CROSS APPLY, and LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true matches OUTER APPLY. PostgreSQL does not accept the APPLY keywords, so rewrite them with LATERAL when you migrate.
Why do I need ON true in a LEFT JOIN LATERAL?
SQL requires every LEFT JOIN to have a join condition. The matching is already done inside the subquery's WHERE clause, so ON true simply says "join every row the subquery returned".
Is a LATERAL join slow?

It runs the subquery once per left row, so it is fast when each run is an index lookup and slow when each run scans a big table. Add an index on the columns the subquery filters and sorts on, and check the plan for an Index Scan on the inner side of the Nested Loop.
Can I use LATERAL with a function in PostgreSQL?

Yes. For a function call in FROM, such as generate_series() or unnest(), the LATERAL keyword is optional because the arguments can already refer to earlier tables. Writing it anyway is allowed and can make the query clearer.
Summary

items.content: LATERAL lets a subquery in FROM use columns from tables listed before it; it runs once per left row.
Without it you get "invalid reference to FROM-clause entry" and a HINT to add LATERAL.
CROSS JOIN LATERAL drops left rows with no matches; LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) alias ON true keeps them with NULLs.
Put ORDER BY ... LIMIT n inside the subquery for top-N per group.
Use LATERAL to return several computed columns at once, or to reuse a calculated value step by step.
For set-returning functions the keyword is optional; for subqueries it is required.
Only INNER and LEFT joins may supply columns to a LATERAL item; RIGHT and FULL raise an error.
Index the child table on (join column, sort column), e.g. (customer_id, order_date DESC), and confirm an Index Scan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

linkedin.post:
Your "latest 2 orders per customer" query fails with: invalid reference to FROM-clause entry. One keyword fixes it.

That keyword is LATERAL. It lets a subquery in FROM use columns from the tables before it, and PostgreSQL runs it once per row on the left.

What to remember:
→ CROSS JOIN LATERAL (...) works like an inner join: customers with no orders disappear.
→ LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) x ON true keeps them, with NULLs.
→ Put ORDER BY ... LIMIT 2 inside the subquery. Then the limit applies per customer, not to the whole result.
→ A LATERAL subquery can return many columns, which a scalar subquery in SELECT cannot ("subquery must return only one column").
→ RIGHT JOIN LATERAL that refers to the left table is rejected: the join must be INNER or LEFT.

Performance: the subquery runs once per left row. Index the child table on (customer_id, order_date DESC). In our test plan, the per-customer Seq Scan plus Sort turned into a single Index Scan.

Coming from SQL Server or Oracle? CROSS APPLY maps to CROSS JOIN LATERAL, and OUTER APPLY maps to LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true.

For top-N per group, which do you reach for first: LATERAL or row_number()?
